extracted.intended_audience: Authors and teams preparing Cochrane systematic reviews of interventions (systematic review authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining the scope and specific questions for Cochrane systematic reviews of interventions, including how to define objectives, use PICO, engage stakeholders, consider equity, and plan methods (e.g. lumping/splitting, logic models, contingencies for sparse data).

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on decision-relevant, answerable questions
rubrics_metrics.description: The focus of any Cochrane review should be on questions that are important to people making decisions about health or health care. Questions should be answerable and fill important gaps in knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well‑formulated questions guide eligibility criteria, searching, data collection, structuring syntheses and presenting findings. They should take into account both benefits and harms of interventions and typically require time, expertise and engagement with intended users.

rubrics_metrics.name: FINER criteria (Feasible, Interesting, Novel, Ethical, Relevant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions should be Feasible, Interesting, Novel, Ethical, and Relevant (FINER).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feasible: team can address question with available evidence and not retrieve unmanageable information; Interest: authors are sufficiently committed; Novel: addresses a genuine gap — check for existing syntheses and PROSPERO; Ethical: consider opportunity costs and political implications; Relevant: involve stakeholders and plan for translation (GRADE considered throughout).

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility (scope and evidence considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: A feasible review asks a question the author team is capable of addressing using the evidence available and not resulting in unmanageable quantities of information or an ‘empty’ review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct up-front scoping to define sensible boundaries; avoid questions that will retrieve unmanageable data or cannot be answered with existing evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty and avoidance of duplication
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel review addresses a genuine gap in knowledge; authors should be aware of related or overlapping reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for pre-existing syntheses in the literature and ongoing reviews in the PROSPERO register before starting to reduce duplication and understand the research context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance and stakeholder engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the review is relevant to stakeholders (consumers, health professionals, policy makers) by involving them in defining focus and questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write up reviews to facilitate translation to decisions; involve stakeholders when prioritising questions and defining exclusions/inclusions; engagement can be ongoing or one-off depending on resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical considerations in question selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider ethics primarily in terms of which questions are prioritised and how they are framed, including potential political implications and impacts on health inequalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for opportunity costs of undertaking the review and consider whether the review could widen or reduce health inequities.

rubrics_metrics.name: MECIR C1: Formulating review questions (Mandatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure that the review question and particularly the outcomes of interest, address issues that are important to review users such as consumers, health professionals and policy makers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cochrane reviews should support practice and policy; consumers play a central role in defining the question. Qualitative research may be used to explore experiences and implementation factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: MECIR C3: Considering potential adverse effects (Mandatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider any important potential adverse effects of the intervention(s) and ensure that they are addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At minimum highlight the extent to which potential adverse effects have been evaluated in included studies. Adverse effect data may come from non-randomized or qualitative studies; this does not mean all reviews must include non-randomized studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aims of intervention reviews (breadth and objectives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic reviews of interventions may focus on a single intervention vs specific comparator or examine a range of interventions (broader reviews).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broader reviews can identify the most effective options and may require network meta-analysis; reviews may also aim to investigate effect modifiers, mechanisms of action, and economic context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective statement format
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement of the review’s objectives should begin with a precise statement of the primary objective, ideally in a single sentence of the form 'To assess the effects of [intervention or comparison] for [health problem] in [types of people, disease or problem and setting if specified]'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow with secondary objectives as needed (different participant groups, comparisons, or outcomes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of PICO and three PICO stages
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the PICO mnemonic (Population, Intervention, Comparison(s), Outcome) and distinguish three stages: review PICO, PICO for each synthesis, and PICO of the included studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review PICO (protocol-stage) defines study eligibility; PICO for each synthesis defines specific synthesis questions and grouping; PICO of included studies is what the studies actually investigated. Decisions on breadth and grouping depend on these levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: MECIR C2: Predefining objectives (Mandatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define in advance the objectives of the review, including population, interventions, comparators and outcomes (PICO).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objectives give focus and must be clear before eligibility criteria can be developed. If multiple interventions are addressed, state how they will be handled (summarised separately, combined, or explicitly compared).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing broad versus narrow scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether the review question should be broad or narrow, considering trade-offs between comprehensiveness and manageability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider generalizability, heterogeneity, resources, interpretability for readers, and potential need for overviews or splitting into multiple reviews. Breadth depends on relevance, theoretical/epidemiological support, validity, and resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-offs table for breadth (population, mode, interventions)
rubrics_metrics.description: When deciding scope consider advantages and disadvantages across dimensions (choice of population, mode of intervention, choice of interventions/comparators).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad scope: comprehensive summary and explore consistency; Disadvantages: more resources, harder interpretation. Narrow scope: manageable and easier to read; Disadvantages: sparse evidence and inability to explore differential effects; risk scope selection could bias results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lumping versus splitting decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide on a continuum between 'lumping' (combining studies in the same analysis) and 'splitting' (separating them); this is different from overall review breadth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions about lumping/splitting for PICO comparisons are driven by review objectives and availability of studies. Lumping can investigate heterogeneity but may produce clinically hard-to-interpret combined effects; splitting reduces heterogeneity but risks too few studies. Consider predefined subgroup analyses, meta-regression, or network meta-analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure review addresses the right questions (priority-setting and stakeholders)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use priority-setting exercises and stakeholder engagement to ensure the review question is meaningful for healthcare decision making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Priorities help prevent waste and increase relevance; translate priorities into answerable PICO questions and recheck with stakeholders. Consider differences across stakeholder groups when deciding inclusions/exclusions and subgroup analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using research priority-setting exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Use existing research priority-setting exercises to define the scope of a review; such exercises decide which uncertainties are most worth resolving through research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search for priority exercises in databases and relevant organisations (e.g. James Lind Alliance, WHO). Translate priorities into PICO format and account for equity when interpreting priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engaging stakeholders to define questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Work with relevant stakeholders (patients/consumers, carers, health professionals, policymakers) to define the review question, especially for health systems and policy reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholder engagement is optimally ongoing throughout the review; benefits include increased relevance, mutual learning and uptake. Identify stakeholders critical to the question and balance resource constraints (one-off vs ongoing engagement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Considering equity when defining questions (PROGRESS-Plus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider in advance whether issues of equity and relevance to specific populations are important, and plan methods to address them; use PROGRESS-Plus to identify socially stratifying factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay attention to low socio-economic groups, low- or middle-income regions, women, children, older people. Where possible include explicit descriptions of intervention effects on disadvantaged groups and plan analyses to examine effects on inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop conceptual framework and prior assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop definitions for key concepts and be clear about prior assumptions (conceptual framework) about why populations are in/out of scope, how the intervention is thought to work, and why outcomes are selected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceptual clarity protects against incoherence and mis-specification of how interventions interact with contexts. These assumptions should be evidenced and their influence assessed when designing eligibility and synthesis plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of specific tools: taxonomies, TIDieR, iCAT_SR, core outcome sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Use taxonomies, generic frameworks (e.g. TIDieR, iCAT_SR), and core outcome sets to categorise interventions, describe intervention characteristics, and identify agreed outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These tools help define scope, group included studies for synthesis, and standardise reporting and descriptions of complex interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic models (purpose and uses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic models are graphical representations of theories about how interventions work, depicting components, mechanisms, outputs and outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Values: refine review questions; decide lumping/splitting; identify components; define eligibility; guide search strategy; explain surrogate outcomes; justify subgroup analyses; enhance policy relevance; structure reporting; illustrate harms/feasibility; interpret results. Develop with stakeholders, update iteratively, and be cautious of oversimplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changing review questions (documentation and guarding against bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions should be posed in the protocol before the full review, but may be refined; any changes should be documented and guarded against bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document protocol changes at the start of Methods; use sensitivity analyses to assess impact. When refining ask: motivation for refinement; whether influenced by included studies; need to modify search/eligibility; appropriateness of data collection; and whether FINER criteria still met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Building contingencies for sparse data
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipate sparse evidence by pre-specifying contingencies in the protocol that allow grouping PICO elements at a broader level to enable synthesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broader groupings address less specific questions (e.g. 'any antioxidant supplement' vs 'vitamin C'). Such approaches can identify leads for future research but may affect certainty-of-evidence assessments (see Chapter 14).

rubrics_metrics.name: Including economic data
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider including economic outcomes (resource use, costs, cost-effectiveness) as part of the review when relevant to decision makers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break down resource use and costs to specific items/categories and consider an international perspective in cost discussions; see Chapter 20 for detailed methods.
